specStatements.text: Students should understand that photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth.

Feeding relationships within a community can be represented by food chains. All food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules. This is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis.
A range of experimental methods using transects and quadrats are used by ecologists to determine the distribution and abundance of species in an ecosystem.

In relation to abundance of organisms students should be able to: understand the terms mean, mode and median; calculate arithmetic means; plot and draw appropriate graphs selecting appropriate scales for the axes.
Producers are eaten by primary consumers, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers.
Consumers that kill and eat other animals are predators, and those eaten are prey. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles.
Students should be able to interpret graphs used to model these cycles.
Students should: recall that many different materials cycle through the abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem; explain the importance of the carbon and water cycles to living organisms.
All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms.
The carbon cycle returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide to be used by plants in photosynthesis.
The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas. Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.
Students are not expected to study the nitrogen cycle.
Students should be able to explain the role of microorganisms in cycling materials through an ecosystem by returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil.
Students should be able to explain how temperature, water and availability of oxygen affect the rate of decay of biological material.

Students should be able to: calculate rate changes in the decay of biological material; translate information between numerical and graphical form; plot and draw appropriate graphs selecting appropriate scales for the axes.
Gardeners and farmers try to provide optimum conditions for rapid decay of waste biological material. The compost produced is used as a natural fertiliser for growing garden plants or crops.
Anaerobic decay produces methane gas. Biogas generators can be used to produce methane gas as a fuel.
Students should be able to evaluate the impact of environmental changes on the distribution of species in an ecosystem given appropriate information.
Environmental changes affect the distribution of species in an ecosystem. These changes include: temperature; availability of water; composition of atmospheric gases.
The changes may be seasonal, geographic or caused by human interaction.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to study the nitrogen cycle.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Students are not expected to study the nitrogen cycle, so nothing in this set mentions nitrogen, nitrates, nitrogen fixation, or nitrifying or denitrifying bacteria. The cycling of materials is covered only through the carbon cycle and the water cycle, and through the role of microorganisms in returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil.

concepts.definition: The organism at the start of a food chain, which synthesises molecules. It is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis. Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth.

A way of representing feeding relationships within a community. All food chains begin with a producer, which is eaten by a primary consumer, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers.
An organism that eats producers. Primary consumers may in turn be eaten by secondary consumers.
An organism that eats primary consumers. Secondary consumers may in turn be eaten by tertiary consumers.
Consumers that kill and eat other animals are predators, and those eaten are prey. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles.

A square frame of known area placed on the ground, used by ecologists to determine the abundance of a species by counting the organisms inside it. Quadrats are placed at random positions so that the sample represents the whole area.
A line marked across a habitat, along which quadrats are placed at intervals. Transects are used by ecologists to determine how the distribution of a species changes across an ecosystem.

The total of all the readings divided by the number of readings, used to summarise the abundance of a species from repeated quadrat counts. It differs from the median, which is the middle value when the readings are put in order, and the mode, which is the most common value.
The non-living (abiotic) and living (biotic) parts of an ecosystem. Many different materials cycle through the abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem.
All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms, rather than being used once and lost.
The cycle that returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis.
The cycle that provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas. Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

The breakdown of dead organisms and waste biological material by microorganisms, which returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil. The rate of decay is affected by temperature, water and the availability of oxygen.
Decay that takes place in the absence of oxygen. Anaerobic decay produces methane gas, and biogas generators can be used to produce methane gas as a fuel.

The material produced when gardeners and farmers provide optimum conditions for rapid decay of waste biological material. The compost is used as a natural fertiliser for growing garden plants or crops.

Where a species is found within an ecosystem. Environmental changes affect the distribution of species; these changes include temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases, and they may be seasonal, geographic or caused by human interaction.

misconceptions.question: Does a food chain have to begin with a producer?
misconceptions.correct: All food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules, usually a green plant or alga.
misconceptions.misconception: A food chain can begin with any organism, so the word producer just means whatever is written first in the chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet food chains as a left-to-right sequence and learn the labels by position rather than by what the organism does, so producer becomes a label for first rather than a description of an organism that synthesises its own molecules.
misconceptions.correction: All food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules. This is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis, so an animal can never be the producer of a chain.

misconceptions.question: Where does a green plant get the biomass it is made of?
misconceptions.correct: A green plant makes glucose by photosynthesis, and photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: Plants take in ready-made food from the soil or the water around them, so the soil is the source of their biomass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language about feeding plants with fertiliser, and the visible fact that roots take up water and mineral ions from soil, make it seem that the plant is taking in food rather than making it.
misconceptions.correction: Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth. The producer synthesises molecules: a green plant or alga makes glucose by photosynthesis, and mineral ions from the soil are not a supply of ready-made food.

misconceptions.question: In the food chain lettuce to slug to hedgehog to fox, which organism is the primary consumer?
misconceptions.correct: The slug is the primary consumer because it eats the producer.
misconceptions.misconception: Consumers are numbered by their position along the chain, so the first organism is the primary consumer, the second is the secondary consumer, and so on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words primary, secondary and tertiary suggest simple counting, and students count every organism in the chain, including the producer, instead of asking what each organism eats.
misconceptions.correction: Producers are eaten by primary consumers, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers. The producer is not counted as a consumer, so in this chain the slug is the primary consumer, the hedgehog the secondary consumer and the fox the tertiary consumer.

misconceptions.question: In a stable community, how do the numbers of predators and prey change over time?
misconceptions.correct: The numbers rise and fall in cycles, with each peak in predator numbers coming after a peak in prey numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey either stay steady or rise and fall together at exactly the same time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read stable as meaning unchanging, and when two curves are drawn on the same axes they are read as one relationship rather than as a delayed response of one population to the other.
misconceptions.correction: In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. More prey allows more predators to be supported, so the peak in predator numbers follows the peak in prey numbers; the larger number of predators then reduces the prey numbers again.

misconceptions.question: A student places quadrats to estimate the abundance of daisies and one quadrat contains no daisies. What should be done with that quadrat?
misconceptions.correct: The zero is recorded and included when the arithmetic mean is calculated.
misconceptions.misconception: Quadrats containing none of the species do not count, so quadrats should be put down where the plants can be seen and empty quadrats should be left out of the mean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A zero looks like a failed reading rather than a result, and students want each quadrat to show them something, so they move the quadrat to a patch of plants or drop the zero when dividing.
misconceptions.correction: Quadrats are used to determine the abundance of a species and are placed at random, so a quadrat containing none of the species is a valid result. The arithmetic mean is the total of all the readings divided by the number of quadrats used, including those that contained none.

misconceptions.question: How is the arithmetic mean of a set of quadrat counts calculated?
misconceptions.correct: The readings are added together and the total is divided by the number of readings.
misconceptions.misconception: Mean, median and mode are just different words for the average, so the middle value or the most common value can be given as the mean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three terms are taught together as types of average and are often asked for in the same question, so students select whichever value is easiest to read off the list instead of carrying out the calculation.
misconceptions.correction: The arithmetic mean is the total of the readings divided by the number of readings. The median is the middle value when the readings are put in order and the mode is the most common value; these are different measures and usually give different answers.

misconceptions.question: How should the scale on the axis of a graph of abundance data be chosen?
misconceptions.correct: The scale should go up in equal steps and should be chosen so that the plotted points fill a good proportion of the grid.
misconceptions.misconception: Any scale can be used on an axis, so the steps can change size along the axis as long as every result fits on the grid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the axis as a list of their own results rather than as a continuous number line, so they write their readings up the side in the order they were recorded, and they choose very large ranges because it feels safe to have room for every value.
misconceptions.correction: When plotting and drawing appropriate graphs, an appropriate scale for the axes goes up in equal steps of a sensible size, and is chosen so that the range of the data fills most of the available grid rather than being squashed into a corner.

misconceptions.question: Which organisms return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: Respiration in animals, plants and microorganisms returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Only animals return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere; plants and microorganisms only take carbon dioxide in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Photosynthesis is learned as the plant reaction that takes in carbon dioxide, and microorganisms are thought of only as things that make material disappear, so both are treated as one-way users of carbon rather than as respiring organisms.
misconceptions.correction: The carbon cycle returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide to be used by plants in photosynthesis. Microorganisms play a key role in cycling materials through an ecosystem by returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide and mineral ions to the soil.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the materials in an organism after it dies, and to the water that drains into the seas?
misconceptions.correct: They are recycled: materials are returned to the ecosystem and water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.
misconceptions.misconception: Materials that leave living organisms are used up and lost from the ecosystem, so water that drains into the seas and carbon locked in dead remains never come back.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Decay and drainage are seen as things disappearing, and students rarely see the return route, so they picture a one-way journey out of the ecosystem instead of a cycle.
misconceptions.correction: All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms. The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas, and water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

misconceptions.question: How does temperature affect the rate of decay of biological material?
misconceptions.correct: Warmth increases the rate of decay up to a point, but very high temperatures denature the enzymes of the microorganisms and slow decay down.
misconceptions.misconception: Decay just needs heat, so the hotter and drier the conditions the faster material will decay.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the rule that raising temperature speeds up reactions without recalling that decay is carried out by living microorganisms with enzymes, and they associate drying with rot being prevented rather than with the microorganisms lacking water.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature, water and the availability of oxygen affect the rate of decay of biological material. A warm temperature increases the rate, but at very high temperatures the enzymes of the microorganisms are denatured, and the microorganisms also need water, so hot dry conditions give slow decay.

misconceptions.question: Why is a biogas generator sealed so that air cannot get in?
misconceptions.correct: Methane gas is produced by anaerobic decay, which happens in the absence of oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: The microorganisms in a biogas generator need a supply of oxygen, because decay always needs oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Decay is first met as rotting in the open air, where the availability of oxygen increases the rate, so students generalise that all decay needs oxygen and overlook anaerobic decay.
misconceptions.correction: Anaerobic decay produces methane gas, and biogas generators can be used to produce methane gas as a fuel. Anaerobic means without oxygen, so the generator is sealed; where oxygen is available, decay produces carbon dioxide rather than methane.

misconceptions.question: The mass of leaf litter in a tray falls from 60 g to 24 g in 12 days. How is the rate of decay calculated?
misconceptions.correct: The change in mass is divided by the time taken, giving 36 g divided by 12 days.
misconceptions.misconception: A rate is a mass divided by a time, so the starting mass or the final mass can be divided by the number of days.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember rate as something over time and reach for the number printed most clearly in the question, without first working out the change in the quantity being measured.
misconceptions.correction: To calculate rate changes in the decay of biological material, work out the change in mass and divide it by the time taken: (60 g minus 24 g) divided by 12 days gives 3 g per day.

misconceptions.question: What kinds of change alter the distribution of species in an ecosystem?
misconceptions.correct: Temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases all affect distribution, and the changes may be seasonal, geographic or caused by human interaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Changes in the distribution of species are caused only by human interaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Environmental change is usually met alongside pollution, deforestation and global warming, so students treat people as the only cause and overlook seasonal and geographic changes that also alter where a species is found.
misconceptions.correction: Environmental changes affect the distribution of species in an ecosystem. These changes include temperature, availability of water and composition of atmospheric gases, and the changes may be seasonal, geographic or caused by human interaction.

misconceptions.question: A species that used to be found across a whole moor is now found only in damp hollows. What does this show?
misconceptions.correct: Its distribution has changed, because conditions are now suitable only in part of the ecosystem.
misconceptions.misconception: If a species is found in a different area than before, the individual organisms must have moved there, or the species must be dying out altogether.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students interpret any change in a species record as a story about the organisms themselves rather than about the conditions, and data showing a smaller area is read as evidence of extinction rather than of a changed distribution.
misconceptions.correction: Environmental changes affect the distribution of species in an ecosystem. When temperature rises or the availability of water falls, a species may survive well only where conditions remain suitable, so its distribution changes even though the species has not died out.

mcqs.stem: How does the producer at the start of a food chain obtain its biomass?

options.text: By taking in ready-made food from soil
options.rationale: A student who believes plants take in ready-made food picks the soil, but the soil supplies water and mineral ions, not food; the producer synthesises its own molecules.

options.text: By feeding on other living organisms
options.rationale: A student who thinks any organism can start a chain accepts a feeding producer, but all food chains begin with a producer which synthesises molecules, not one that eats.

options.text: By using photosynthesis to make glucose
options.rationale: Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth: the producer is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis.

options.text: By absorbing ready-made food in water
options.rationale: A student who believes food is taken in ready-made transfers that idea to algae in water, but an alga also makes its own glucose by photosynthesis.

mcqs.stem: In the food chain lettuce → slug → hedgehog → fox, the hedgehog is:

options.text: a secondary consumer in the chain
options.rationale: Producers are eaten by primary consumers, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers: the hedgehog eats the slug, which is the primary consumer.

options.text: a tertiary consumer in the chain
options.rationale: A student who numbers consumers by position counts the lettuce as the first consumer, making the hedgehog third; the producer is not counted as a consumer.

options.text: a primary consumer in the chain
options.rationale: A student who counts only the animals that hunt makes the hedgehog the first, but a primary consumer is an organism that eats producers, which the hedgehog does not.

options.text: a producer of biomass in the chain
options.rationale: A student who treats producer as a loose label applies it to an animal, but producers synthesise molecules by photosynthesis and are found at the start of the chain.

mcqs.stem: A graph for a stable community shows that each peak in the number of lynx comes about a year after a peak in the number of hares. What does the graph show?

options.text: Predator numbers peak before prey numbers
options.rationale: A student who does not read the order of the peaks reverses the relationship; the graph shows the lynx peak, and lynx are the predators, coming later than the hare peak.

options.text: Predator numbers peak with the prey numbers
options.rationale: A student who thinks the two populations change together ignores the one-year gap that the graph shows between the two peaks.

options.text: Predator numbers stay level as prey cycle
options.rationale: A student who reads stable as unchanging expects a flat predator line, but in a stable community the numbers of both predators and prey rise and fall in cycles.

options.text: Predator numbers peak after prey numbers
options.rationale: In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles; more prey supports more predators, so the peak in predator numbers follows the peak in prey numbers.

mcqs.stem: A student places five quadrats at random in a field and counts the daisies in each: 7, 0, 6, 7, 5. What is the mean number of daisies per quadrat?

options.text: 6.0 daisies per quadrat
options.rationale: This is the median, the middle value when the counts are put in order; the mean is the total of the readings divided by the number of readings.

options.text: 7.0 daisies per quadrat
options.rationale: This is the mode, the most common value; the mode is not the same measure as the arithmetic mean and here it is higher than it.

options.text: 5.0 daisies per quadrat
options.rationale: The arithmetic mean is the total of the readings divided by the number of readings: 25 daisies divided by 5 quadrats gives 5.0 daisies per quadrat.

options.text: 6.25 daisies per quadrat
options.rationale: This comes from leaving out the quadrat containing no daisies and dividing by four; a zero is a valid result and must be included in the mean.

mcqs.stem: Counts of daisies per quadrat range from 2 to 46. Which scale should the student use on the y-axis when plotting these results?

options.text: 0 to 50, using steps of 2, 5, 10
options.rationale: A student who treats the axis as a list of results changes the step size along it, but unequal steps distort the plotted points and the shape of the graph.

options.text: 0 to 50, using equal steps of 5
options.rationale: An appropriate scale goes up in equal steps and lets the range of the data fill most of the grid, so all counts from 2 to 46 can be plotted accurately.

options.text: 0 to 500, using equal steps of 50
options.rationale: The steps are equal but the scale is ten times too large, so all the points are squashed into the bottom of the grid and cannot be plotted or read accurately.

options.text: 2 to 46, using steps of 4 then 10
options.rationale: A student who starts the axis at the first reading and changes the step part way up produces an axis that is not a continuous, evenly divided scale.

mcqs.stem: What is the role of microorganisms in cycling materials through an ecosystem?

options.text: They take in carbon dioxide from the air and ions from soil
options.rationale: A student who thinks only animals release carbon dioxide has microorganisms taking it in, but microorganisms respire and return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

options.text: They return carbon dioxide to the air and ions to the soil
options.rationale: Microorganisms cycle materials by returning carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis, and mineral ions to the soil.

options.text: They remove carbon dioxide and mineral ions from this cycle
options.rationale: A student who thinks decayed materials are lost has them leaving the cycle, but all materials in the living world are recycled as building blocks for future organisms.

options.text: They lock carbon dioxide and mineral ions in the dead matter
options.rationale: A student who sees decay as material disappearing keeps the carbon and mineral ions shut away, but decay is what releases them back into the ecosystem.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes how the water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land?

options.text: Salt water drains from the seas onto the land
options.rationale: A student who does not see a return route through the atmosphere has the seas flowing back inland, but water reaches the land as precipitation, and it is fresh.

options.text: Water used up by organisms is lost from the land
options.rationale: A student who believes materials are used once treats water in organisms as gone, but that water is also evaporated and precipitated and so is recycled.

options.text: Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated
options.rationale: The water cycle provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas, because water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.

options.text: Water is lost to the seas and is not returned
options.rationale: A student who sees drainage as a one-way journey stops the cycle at the sea, but water is continuously evaporated from the seas and precipitated again.

mcqs.stem: A gardener wants rapid decay of waste plant material in a compost heap, to use the compost as a natural fertiliser. Which conditions give the fastest rate of decay?

options.text: Very hot, dry, with oxygen present
options.rationale: A student who thinks hotter is faster without limit chooses this, but very high temperatures denature the enzymes of the microorganisms and they also need water.

options.text: Warm, moist and with oxygen present
options.rationale: Temperature, water and the availability of oxygen affect the rate of decay, so gardeners provide optimum conditions: warm, moist and with oxygen available.

options.text: Warm, moist and with oxygen kept out
options.rationale: A student who is unsure about oxygen removes it, but without oxygen the material decays anaerobically and more slowly, producing methane rather than compost quickly.

options.text: Warm, dry and with oxygen present
options.rationale: A student who thinks only temperature matters ignores water, but microorganisms need water to decay biological material, so dry material decays slowly.

mcqs.stem: In an investigation the mass of leaf litter in a tray fell from 60 g to 24 g in 12 days. What was the mean rate of decay?

options.text: 3.0 g per day
options.rationale: The rate change in decay is the change in mass divided by the time taken: 60 g minus 24 g is 36 g, and 36 g divided by 12 days is 3.0 g per day.

options.text: 2.0 g per day
options.rationale: This divides the final mass by the time; a rate of decay uses the change in mass, not the mass that is left at the end.

options.text: 5.0 g per day
options.rationale: This divides the starting mass by the time; only the 36 g that has decayed has been lost over the 12 days.

options.text: 36.0 g per day
options.rationale: This is the change in mass with no division by time, so it is a mass and not a rate; the change happened over 12 days.

mcqs.stem: Why must a biogas generator be sealed so that air cannot get in?

options.text: Methane is produced by anaerobic decay
options.rationale: Anaerobic decay produces methane gas, so a biogas generator is sealed to keep oxygen out and produce methane gas that can be used as a fuel.

options.text: Methane is produced faster in warmer air
options.rationale: A student who explains every change in decay by temperature alone chooses warmth, but sealing the generator controls oxygen, not how warm the material is.

options.text: Oxygen is needed to produce the methane
options.rationale: A student who believes decay always needs oxygen gives the opposite of the reason for sealing it; methane is produced by anaerobic decay, without oxygen.

options.text: Bacteria need air to produce the methane
options.rationale: A student who pictures rotting in the open air supplies the microorganisms with air, but these microorganisms decay the material in the absence of oxygen.

mcqs.stem: Thirty years ago a moss grew across a whole moor. Mean summer temperature has since risen and summer rainfall has fallen, and the moss is now found only in damp hollows. Which conclusion is best supported by this information?

options.text: Human interaction has removed it from this moor
options.rationale: A student who treats people as the only cause looks past the data, which describe changes in temperature and rainfall, not any human activity on the moor.

options.text: The species is dying out across the whole moor
options.rationale: A student who reads a smaller area as extinction overstates the evidence; the moss is still growing where the conditions remain suitable.

options.text: The plants moved downhill into the damp hollows
options.rationale: A student who pictures organisms travelling misreads the data; the distribution has changed because the moss survives only where water is still available.

options.text: The availability of water limits its distribution
options.rationale: Environmental changes including temperature and availability of water affect the distribution of species, and the moss is now found only where water remains available.
